```{python}
import pandas as pd
```

```{python}
%%R
files <- list.files("data/output", pattern = "^data-[0-9]{4}\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

hcris.data <- purrr::map_dfr(files, ~ {
  readr::read_csv(.x, show_col_types = FALSE)
})

kff.data <- readr::read_tsv(
  "data/input/medicaid_expansion.txt",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(
    expand_year = lubridate::year(as.Date(date_adopted)),
    expand_ever = expanded
  )

state.xwalk <- tibble(
  state = c(state.abb, "DC"),
  State = c(state.name, "District of Columbia")
)

hcris.data <- hcris.data %>%
  left_join(state.xwalk, by = "state") %>%
  left_join(
    kff.data %>% select(State, expand_ever, expand_year),
    by = "State"
  ) %>%
  mutate(uncomp_care_mill = uncomp_care / 1e6)

sort(unique(hcris.data$year))
```

# Summarize the data

## Question 1
### Provide a table of mean hospital uncompensated care (in millions of dollars) by year, from 2010 through 2018. How has uncompensated care changed over time?

```{python}
%%R -o q1_table
q1.table <- hcris.data %>%
  filter(year >= 2011, year <= 2018, uncomp_care > 0) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(
    `Mean Uncomp Care ($M)` = mean(uncomp_care_mill, na.rm = TRUE),
    Hospitals = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

q1_table <- q1.table
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd

q1_table = pd.DataFrame(q1_table)
q1_table = q1_table.round(2)
q1_table
```

## Question 2
### Plot mean uncompensated care over time separately for states that expanded Medicaid in 2014 versus states that never expanded. Drop all states that expanded after 2014. Does the graph suggest a potential treatment effect?

```{python}
%%R
plot.data <- hcris.data %>%
  filter(year >= 2011, year <= 2018, uncomp_care > 0) %>%
  filter(is.na(expand_year) | expand_year == 2014) %>%
  group_by(expand_ever, year) %>%
  summarize(mean_uncomp = mean(uncomp_care_mill, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(group_label = if_else(expand_ever, "Expansion", "Non-expansion"))

ggplot(plot.data, aes(x = year, y = mean_uncomp, group = expand_ever, linetype = expand_ever)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2013.5, color = "red") +
  geom_text(
    data = plot.data %>% filter(year == 2016),
    aes(label = group_label, x = year + 0.7, y = mean_uncomp),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean Uncompensated Care ($M)")
```

## Question 3
### Using 2012 and 2015 as your pre and post periods, present a 2x2 DD table of mean uncompensated care for expansion versus non-expansion states (again focusing only on 2014 expanders and never-expanders).

```{python}
%%R -o dd_table_wide -o dd.est.manual
dd.table <- hcris.data %>%
  filter(uncomp_care > 0) %>%
  filter(is.na(expand_year) | expand_year == 2014) %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2015)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(expand_ever)) %>%
  group_by(expand_ever, year) %>%
  summarize(uncomp = mean(uncomp_care_mill, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

dd.table.wide <- pivot_wider(dd.table, names_from = "year",
                              names_prefix = "year", values_from = "uncomp") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(expand_ever = case_when(
    expand_ever == FALSE ~ "Non-expansion",
    expand_ever == TRUE  ~ "Expansion"
  )) %>%
  rename(Group = expand_ever, Pre = year2012, Post = year2015)

dd.est.manual <- (dd.table.wide$Post[dd.table.wide$Group == "Expansion"] -
                   dd.table.wide$Pre[dd.table.wide$Group == "Expansion"]) -
                  (dd.table.wide$Post[dd.table.wide$Group == "Non-expansion"] -
                   dd.table.wide$Pre[dd.table.wide$Group == "Non-expansion"])
dd_table_wide <- dd.table.wide
dd_est_manual <- dd.est.manual
```

```{python}
dd_table_wide = pd.DataFrame(dd_table_wide).round(2)
dd_table_wide
```

## Question 4
### Briefly discuss what policies or events might explain the trends you observe. Why might we expect Medicaid expansion to affect uncompensated care?

#### Medicaid expansion extends insurance coverage to low-income adults who were previously uninsured. When these individuals visit hospitals, they now have Medicaid coverage rather than presenting as uninsured. This shifts the payer mix, reducing the volume of care for which hospitals receive no reimbursement (uncompensated care). In addition, the ACA marketplace subsidies and the individual mandate (in effect through 2018) reduced the overall uninsured population, which would also lower uncompensated care even in non-expansion states. However, the larger reduction in expansion states is consistent with Medicaid expansion playing a distinct role beyond these general ACA effects.

# Estimate ATEs

## Question 5
### Estimate the effect of Medicaid expansion on hospital uncompensated care using a standard DD regression estimator, focusing only on states that expanded in 2014 versus those that never expanded.


```{python}
%%R
reg.data <- hcris.data %>%
  filter(uncomp_care > 0) %>%
  filter(is.na(expand_year) | expand_year == 2014) %>%
  filter(year >= 2011, year <= 2018) %>%
  mutate(post = (year >= 2014),
         treat = post * expand_ever)

dd.est <- lm(uncomp_care_mill ~ post + expand_ever + treat, data = reg.data)
```

```{python}
%%R -o q5_table
q5_table <- as.data.frame(coef(summary(dd.est)))
q5_table$term <- rownames(q5_table)
rownames(q5_table) <- NULL
```

```{python}
q5_table = pd.DataFrame(q5_table).round(3)
q5_table
```

## Question 6
### Include hospital and year fixed effects in your estimates using the fixest package. Cluster your standard errors at the state level. How do your results compare to those in question 5?

```{python}
%%R
fe.est <- feols(uncomp_care_mill ~ treat | provider_number + year,
                cluster = ~state, data = reg.data)
```

```{python}
%%R -o q6_table
q6_table <- as.data.frame(coeftable(fe.est))
q6_table$term <- rownames(q6_table)
rownames(q6_table) <- NULL
```

```{python}
compare_q5_q6_wide = compare_q5_q6.pivot(index="term", columns="model")
compare_q5_q6_wide = compare_q5_q6_wide.round(3)
compare_q5_q6_wide
```

## Question 7
### Repeat the analysis in question 6 but include all states (even those that expanded after 2014). Are your results different? If so, why?

```{python}
%%R
reg.data2 <- hcris.data %>%
  filter(uncomp_care > 0) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010, year <= 2018) %>%
  mutate(treat = case_when(
    year >= expand_year & !is.na(expand_year) ~ 1,
    is.na(expand_year) ~ 0,
    year < expand_year & !is.na(expand_year) ~ 0
  ))

fe.est2 <- feols(uncomp_care_mill ~ treat | provider_number + year,
                 cluster = ~state, data = reg.data2)
```

```{python}
%%R -o q7_table
q7_table <- as.data.frame(coeftable(fe.est2))
q7_table$term <- rownames(q7_table)
rownames(q7_table) <- NULL
```

```{python}
q7_table = pd.DataFrame(q7_table).round(3)
q7_table["term"] = q7_table["term"].replace({"treat": "Post x Expansion"})
q7_table
```

#### The estimate for question 7 is around 3 points greater than the estimate for question 6. In fact, the question 7 estimate is actually the most resemblant of question 5 (both around -22.9). When we include all states, we would see that the amount of uncompensated care is still lower for expansion states, but not as low as for 6. This is because the impact of an expansion policy takes time to truly start seeing effects. When we account for all states that expanded, even the later ones, these are states that have not yet seen all of the benefits of expansion. 

## Question 8
### Provide an “event study” graph showing the effects of Medicaid expansion in each year. Use the specification that includes hospital and year fixed effects, limited to states that expanded in 2014 or never expanded (with 2013 as the reference year).

```{python}
%%R
mod.twfe <- feols(uncomp_care_mill ~ i(year, expand_ever, ref = 2013) |
                    provider_number + year,
                  cluster = ~state, data = reg.data)
```

```{python}
%%R
iplot(mod.twfe,
      xlab = "Year",
      main = "")
```

## Question 9
### Repeat part 8 but include all states that expanded after 2014. You will need to construct an “event time” variable and bin end points as discussed in class.

```{python}
%%R
reg.data2 <- reg.data2 %>%
  mutate(time_to_treat = ifelse(expand_ever == TRUE, year - expand_year, -1),
         time_to_treat = ifelse(time_to_treat <= -4, -4, time_to_treat))

mod.twfe2 <- feols(uncomp_care_mill ~ i(time_to_treat, expand_ever, ref = -1) |
                     provider_number + year,
                   cluster = ~state, data = reg.data2)
```

```{python}
%%R
iplot(mod.twfe2,
      xlab = "Time to Treatment",
      main = "")
```

## Question 10
### Summarize your findings from questions 5-9. What is the effect of Medicaid expansion on hospital uncompensated care? Do the event study graphs suggest any concerns about the parallel trends assumption? Briefly discuss one limitation of the standard TWFE estimator in the context of staggered Medicaid expansion.

####
Across specifications, we find that Medicaid expansion reduced hospital uncompensated care. The event study with common treatment timing shows pre-2014 coefficients close to zero, supporting the parallel trends assumption. Post-2014, expansion states experience statistically significant declines in uncompensated care relative to non-expansion states.

The staggered event study tells a similar story, with pre-treatment coefficients near zero and negative post-treatment effects. However, one important limitation of the standard TWFE estimator in the staggered setting is that it uses already-treated units as controls for later-treated units. This can produce biased estimates when treatment effects are heterogeneous over time, because the "control" group includes hospitals that have already been affected by expansion. Recent econometric work (e.g., Callaway and Sant'Anna, Sun and Abraham, de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille) has developed alternative estimators that avoid this problem by restricting comparisons to not-yet-treated or never-treated units.
